overview.body:
**Omononushi** ​(*omononushi*) — ‌Mountains, ‌Deity of ​Miwa · ​Great ​thing lord ​— ​belongs to ‌the Japanese ​tradition, ​where it ‌is ​catalogued under ‌the ​domain "Mountains, ‌Deity of ​Miwa". ​The name ​means ​"Great thing ​lord"[^1].

‌**Ōmononushi** is ​the mysterious ‌kami ​of Mount ‌Miwa, ​one of ‌the oldest ​and ‌most enigmatic ​deities ​in Japan. ‌He ‌is associated ‌with snakes, ​oracles, ​and the ‌transfer ​of the ​land ‌to Amaterasu's ​descendants. Unlike ​most ‌kami, he ​had ‌no image ​and was ​worshipped ​in the ​form ‌of the ‌mountain ​itself.[^2]

PuniCodex ‌restores the ​name ​as **Omononushi** ‌and ‌serves its ‌temple ‌at [its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/omononushi/). The ‌restoration ​aSCII-equivalent form ​— ​a description ‌computed from ​the ​displayed form ​itself. ‌The plain ​ASCII ​form *omononushi* ​survives as ‌a ​modern convenience ‌imposed ​by the ‌early ​domain-name system; ‌the restoration, ‌not ​the fallback, ​is ​the form ​the project ‌defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in ​Japanese characters ​as ​**大物忌神**. Etymologically ​it ​means ‌"Great thing ​lord"[^1].

​The ASCII ‌form ​*omononushi* survives ‌only ​because ‌the early ​domain-name ​system could ​not ​carry ​diacritics; it ‌is ​a technological ‌compromise, ​not ‌an ancient ​spelling. ‌The Unicode ​restoration ‌**Omononushi** ​recovers the ​full ‌diacritic detail ‌of ‌the scholarly ​transliteration ​directly ‌in the ​address ​bar. The ‌restoration ​aSCII-equivalent ​form — ‌a ​description computed ‌from ​the ​displayed form ​itself.

​The letter-by-letter ‌transformation ‌runs:

- ​**o** → ‌**O** ​— Same, ​capitalized
- ‌**m** → ‌**m** ‌— ‌Same
- **o** ​→ ‌**o** — ​Same
- ​**n** ​→ **n** ‌— ​Same

pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of ‌the ​name is ​**/o.mo.no.nɯ.ɕi/** ​— Modern ​Standard ​Japanese (Hepburn).[^1]

‌Phoneme ​by ​phoneme:

- **O-** ‌— ​Open-mid back ‌[o]
- ​**-mo-** — ‌Bilabial ​[m] ​plus open-mid ​[o]; ​from 物 ​'thing'
- ‌**-no-** ​— Alveolar ‌nasal ​[n] plus ‌open-mid ​[o]
- **-nushi** ‌— ​Alveolar ‌nasal [n], ​close ​back [ɯ], ‌voiceless ‌alveolo-palatal [ɕ], ‌close ​front ​[i]; from ‌主 ​'lord/master'

For ​the ‌modern ​speaker, the ​closest ‌approximation is: ​'OH-moh-noh-noo-shee' ‌— even ​syllables, ​with ​soft final ​vowels.

‌Kindred and ‌historical ​forms ‌of the ​name:

- ​**Japanese** — ‌大物忌神 ‌(Ōmononushi-no-kami), 'Great ‌Thing ‌Lord'
- ​**Other names** ‌— ​Miwa-no-kami; identified ​with ​Ōkuninushi (Ōnamuji) ‌in ​some ​traditions
- **Cult ​center** ‌— Ōmiwa ​Shrine ​at ​Mount Miwa, ‌Nara

​Omononushi keeps ‌its ​restoration plain: ‌plain ​Hepburn. ‌He is ‌an ​ancient mountain ​deity ​associated with ​Miwa ‌and ‌the land-transfer ​myth.

domains.body:
**Ōmononushi** ​is the ‌mysterious ‌kami of ​Mount ​Miwa, one ​of ​the oldest ​and most ‌enigmatic ​deities in ​Japan. ‌He is ​associated ‌with snakes, ​oracles, ‌and the ​transfer ​of the ​land ​to Amaterasu's ​descendants. ‌Unlike most ​kami, he ‌had ​no image ‌and ​was worshipped ‌in ​the form ‌of ​the mountain ​itself.[^1]

### ‌Mountain God

‌He ‌is identified ​with ​Mount Miwa ‌itself; Ōmiwa ​Shrine ​has no ‌inner ​sanctuary because ​the ‌peak is ​the ‌kami's body.

### ​Snake ​Deity

He ​comes ​to Ikutamayori ‌as a ‌serpent ​in the ‌Kojiki, ​and snake ​offerings ‌of sake ‌attend ‌his Miwa ‌cult.

### ​Oracle Kami

‌His ​consent to ​the ​land-transfer was ‌given by ​oracle ​— sovereignty ​in ‌Japan changes ​hands ​by consultation, ​not ‌conquest.

### Land ​Transfer

‌He is ​the ‌voice that ​yields ‌the land ‌to the ​heavenly ​descendants, binding ​the ​Miwa line ‌to ‌the imperial ​house.

symbols.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated ‌with ​Omononushi ​concentrates ​in ​a small ​set ‌of ​recurring ​attributes, ‌each ​a ‌compressed ​statement ‌about ​the ​name:[^1]

- ​**Mount ​Miwa** ​— ‌The mountain ​itself, ‌worshipped ​as ‌the ​kami's ‌body ​— ‌his ​true ​shintai
- ‌**Snake** ‌— ‌The ​form ​in which ‌Ōmononushi ​appears ​in ‌the ​Ikutamayori ​legend ‌— ​the ‌sacred ​without ​a ​face
- ​**Sake** ‌— Offered ‌to ​the ‌serpent-kami; ​Ōmononushi ​is ‌patron ‌of ‌the ‌brewers ​of ‌Miwa, ​honored ​with ​sugitama ‌cedar balls
- ​**The ​Miwa-torii** ​— ‌The ​unique ​three-pillared ​torii ‌through ​which ‌worshippers ​face ‌the ​peak ‌directly ‌— architecture ​that ​frames ​a ​god ‌who ‌is ​geology

mythology.body:
Ōmononushi's mythology is preserved in ​strange, archaic tales of snakes, possession, and oracles — ‌the Kojiki's strangest marriage, the constitution of Japan's ‌sovereignty, and a shrine with no god-house, because the ​mountain is the god.[^1]

### The Serpent Husband of Ikutamayori ​(Kojiki)

A maiden named Ikutamayori was visited each ​night by a beautiful man who came unseen. When ​she bore his child, her parents demanded to know ​the father. She had him leave a needle ‌threaded with red silk in the hem of his ​garment; in the morning she followed the thread, and ​it led to the foot of Mount Miwa ‌and vanished into a cave — where the visitor ​declared himself: he was *Ōmononushi*, the great lord of ‌the mountain, and he appeared in serpent form. ​The child of this union was Kotoshironushi, the god ‌who would one day counsel the peaceful surrender of ​the land to the heavenly grandson (Kojiki; cf. ​Nihon Shoki, Aston's translation).

The tale binds three things ​into one knot — mountain, snake, and the Miwa ​priestly line, whose descent from the kami's human ​bride it exists to explain.[^2]

### The Oracle of the ‌Land (Kojiki · Nihon Shoki)

When the heavenly emissary ​Takemikazuchi descended to demand the land from the ‌earthly god Ōnamuji (Ōkuninushi), Ōnamuji consulted his children. Kotoshironushi, ​away at Cape Miwa, answered that resistance to the ‌heavenly grandson was hopeless — and then all ​eyes turned to the mountain. Ōmononushi was consulted, and ‌his oracle settled the matter: 'Let the land be ​given over in peace,' he declared; the land ‌was yielded, and he withdrew into a hidden realm, ​promising that his favor would attend his proper worship. ​The Nihon Shoki tells the same event differently, ‌folding the mountain god into Ōnamuji himself: Ōnamuji, it ‌says, is also called Ōmononushi (Kojiki; Nihon Shoki, tr. ‌Aston, I).

Here the god is pure voice: ​sovereignty changes hands in Japan not by conquest but ​by consultation — and the mountain kami's consent is ‌the constitution.

### The Bride of Miwa (Kojiki)

Ōmononushi ​took as wife Seyadatarahime, daughter of his own son ​Kotoshironushi by Ikutamayori — and their child was the ‌princess Himetataraisuzuhime. She became the consort of Emperor ​Sujin and bore the future Emperor Suinin: the serpent-god ​of Mount Miwa thus entered the imperial genealogy itself, ‌the god's line becoming grandmother to the next ​sovereign. The Kojiki's genealogy is compressed and the texts ‌do not spell every step out plainly, but the ​dynastic point stands: the mountain married into the ​house that received the mountain's realm.

The marriage also ​sealed an alliance between the Miwa priestly house and ​the court — the god who gave the ‌land away kept his blood beside the throne. The ‌Kojiki records the whole sequence without wonder, as plain ​genealogy: which is how one knows the text ‌was compiled on the winning side.

### The Plague and ​the Possessed Princess (Kojiki · Nihon Shoki)

In Emperor ​Sujin's reign plague and disaster struck the land, ‌and divination named the cause: the great kami of ‌Mount Miwa, never yet given a shrine, was angry. ‌The god made his will known by possessing ‌a princess of his own line and speaking through ​her: worship me, he demanded, and I will cause ‌the land to flourish. Sujin founded the rites; ​the pestilence lifted. The Nihon Shoki's parallel account likewise ​has the god speak through a human mouth, claim ​credit for guiding the cession of the land, ‌and demand his due — the god of Miwa ​and the god of the land-transfer asserted as one ​and the same (Kojiki; Nihon Shoki, Aston I).

​Myth here explains a liturgy: Ōmiwa's worship began, the ‌texts insist, when the neglected mountain finally raised its ​voice.

### Worship without Image (Cult)

Ōmiwa Shrine, at ​the foot of the mountain in Nara prefecture, is ​one of Japan's oldest shrines and one of the ‌strangest: it has no *honden*, no inner sanctuary ​housing a divine image, because the god is not ‌symbolized by anything — the god *is* Mount Miwa. ​Worshippers pray toward the peak across a unique ‌three-pillared torii, the Miwa-torii; before the worship hall stand ​sacred sake casks, for Ōmononushi is patron of the ‌brewers of Miwa, and his serpent form — ‌a great snake said to coil in the mountain's ​caves — was traditionally offered sake. First listed among ​the great shrines in the Engishiki (927 CE), ​the site preserves a stratum of Japanese religion older ​than images: the mountain itself as *shintai*, the deity's ‌body.

The absent statue is the theology: what ‌has no face cannot be owned, and what cannot ​be owned cannot be conquered.

syncretism.body:
Ōmononushi ​never left ‌Shinto, but ‌he was ​folded into ​it from ​two directions. ​The Nihon ​Shoki already ‌identifies him ​with Ōkuninushi ​— ‌the local ​Miwa kami ‌gathered into ​the imperial ‌land-myth — ​and medieval ​*honji suijaku* ​doctrine went ​further: Mount ​Miwa's deity, ‌as ​Miwa Daimyōjin, ‌was given ​the Buddhist ‌original ground ​of Śākyamuni ‌Buddha, and ​Miwa mandalas ‌picture the ​mountain with ​Buddhist cosmography ‌laid ‌over it. ‌Under the ​mountain, ascetics ​of the ‌Shugendō tradition ​practiced until ​the modern ‌period, treating ​the peak ​itself as ‌the ​object of ‌cult. The ​serpent, the ​sake, and ​the oracle ​— archaic, ‌local, and ‌oracular — ​are precisely ‌the features ​a ​centralizing mythology ‌needed to ‌absorb rather ‌than erase: ‌Ōmononushi survives ​because he ‌was useful, ​first to ​the court ​that took ‌his ​oracle, then ​to the ​Buddhism that ‌crowned him, ​then to ​the brewers ​who still ‌hang cedar ​balls for ‌him.[^1]

Kindred ​figures ‌in the ​PuniCodex cross-tradition ‌index include ‌[[anahita|Anāhitā]], [[audhumla|Auðhumla]], ​[[babaluaye|Ọbalúayé]], [[bastet|Bꜣstt]], ​[[cernunnos|Cernunnos]], and ​[[coatlicue|Cōātlīcue]], each ​linked through ‌earth / ‌mother / ​fertility.

cultural-legacy.body: Ōmiwa ​Shrine still ‌stands ‌where the ​myth ​says ​it must: ​at ​the foot ‌of ​Mount Miwa, ​without ‌a main ​hall, ‌prayer ​aimed at ‌the ​peak. The ​surrounding ​district remains ​sacred ​geography — ‌Isonokami, ​one ‌of Japan's ​oldest ‌shrines, close ​by, ‌and the ​great ‌early kofun ​of ​Hashihaka ‌on the ‌horizon. ‌Miwa sake ​is ​still brewed ‌under ​the god's ​patronage, ‌and ​brewers across ​Japan ‌hang *sugitama* ​cedar ‌balls in ​his ​honor. ​The mountain ​appears ‌in Nara-period ‌poetry, ​and the ‌Miwa-torii's ​third pillar ​is ‌studied ‌wherever shrine ‌architecture ‌is taught. ​For ‌modern Shinto, ​Ōmononushi ​is the ​standing ‌proof ​that the ​kami ​need not ‌be ​anthropomorphic: his ​'image' ​is a ‌modest ​ridge ‌of green ​rock ‌and cedar, ​and ‌on clear ‌mornings ​the faithful ​still ​bow ​toward it ‌before ‌entering the ​shrine.[^1]

archaeology.body: The ​Engishiki shrine ‌register ‌(927 ​CE) already ​lists ​Ōmiwa ​among the ​great ‌sanctuaries, ​and the ​site's ‌archaeology is ​deep: ‌excavations ​around Miwa ‌have ​yielded ​ritual deposits ​and ​prestige ​objects — ‌bronze ​mirrors, swords, ‌and ​beads ‌— from ​the ‌Yayoi-to-Kofun ​transition, indicating ‌a ​sanctuary ​of unusual ‌antiquity ‌at the ‌mountain's ​foot, ​and the ‌great ​keyhole ​tomb Hashihaka ‌nearby ​marks ​the district ‌as ​an early ‌center ​of ​power. No ​honden ​has ‌ever stood ‌at ​Ōmiwa; ‌worship runs ​toward ​the peak ‌through ‌the ‌unique Miwa-torii, ‌whose ​third ‌central pillar ​frames ​the ​mountain as ‌the ​true sanctuary. ​The ​'artifact' ‌of this ​god ​is ​thus geological ‌and ​botanical ‌at once ​— ‌bedrock, cedar, ​and ‌the ‌spring-water sake ​that ​the ​shrine has ​brewed ‌since ‌the rite ​began.[^1]

meditation.body: Ōmononushi ​is the ‌god who ‌refuses to ​be a ​person. Every ​other great ​kami ​of Japan ‌acquired a ​face, a ​genealogy, a ‌palace in ​the poems; ‌Ōmononushi ​acquired a ‌mountain, and ​the mountain ​— unportable, ​unburnable, unshippable ​— ​has guarded ‌his integrity ​ever since. ‌He enters ​myth only ‌as a ​voice ‌or a ​snake: the ‌two forms ​in which ​the sacred ‌appears without ‌becoming ‌an idol. ​His oracle ​teaches a ‌politics as ​well: the ​land changed ‌hands ​because he ​consented, and ‌consent, not ​conquest, is ‌what his ​cult ​claims as ​the first ​principle of ‌sovereignty. Even ‌his marriage ​reads like ‌an ​essay in ​legitimacy, wedding ‌the mountain's ‌line to ‌the dynasty ‌that received ​the ‌mountain's realm. ​And because ​there is ​no statue, ‌every visit ​to Ōmiwa ​is ​a small ‌reenactment of ​the discovery ​of the ​sacred — ‌you ​look up ‌from the ​torii, past ‌the sake ​casks, at ‌green rock ‌and ​cedar, and ​understand that ​you have ​been inside ‌the shrine ‌since the ​road.[^1]

kojiki-nihonshoki.body:
Japan's two earliest chronicles, the Kojiki (712 CE) and Nihon Shoki (720 CE), record Omononushi in mythic narratives of cosmogony and imperial descent. The name appears in kanji logographs whose readings were later fixed by tradition.

The restoration Omononushi preserves the romanized scholarly form derived from those classical sources.[^1]

shinto-sources.body:
Shinto ritual texts, shrine records, and norito prayers preserve the cultic identity of Omononushi. The kami is honored at shrines associated with mountains, and festival calendars perpetuate the name.

The Unicode form Omononushi gives that ongoing tradition a precise digital address.[^1]

buddhist-japanese.body:
Japanese Buddhist literature and art sometimes assimilate Omononushi into Buddhist cosmology, mapping kami onto dharmic protectors and bodhisattvas. The honji-suijaku discourse provides a framework for such identifications.

The restored name Omononushi appears in both Shinto and Buddhist contexts in the PuniCodex archive.[^1]
